prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map supports a layered layout: the camera wearer’s knees, hands, bag, and reading material occupy the near foreground (roughly 0.3–0.8 m), the grass extends several metres ahead, and the rock barrier and water lie farther away (about 5–10 m and beyond). Across the five frames, the foreground objects shift from a bag and hand on the lower right/centre, to legs and handheld items near the lower edge, and finally to an open book at lower right; these changes appear driven mainly by head/camera rotation rather than clear approach or retreat. The map makes relative distance and occlusion clearer than RGB—foreground legs, hands, bag, and pages appear bright and interrupt the more distant grass—while objects near one another in the lower frame are within the wearer’s arm’s reach. Absolute metre estimates are uncertain, the upper border contains irregular black invalid regions, and several distant surfaces have overly smooth or inconsistent depth, so it does not reliably establish distances between the small faraway figures or whether they face the wearer.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map separates nearby instances along the lower edge: several person masks corresponding largely to the wearer’s visible legs/body, a handbag or suitcase at lower left/centre, cellphones near the hands in the middle frames, a tennis-racket label near the lower centre, and a book at lower right in the last frame. Their positions show the camera turning across time: the bag begins left of the wearer’s near body, handheld objects appear near the centre-right in intermediate frames, and the book becomes the dominant near object on the right; overlapping masks indicate partial occlusion by hands, legs, or frame boundaries. The isolated tiny labels high in the first two frames imply distant detections, but the labels “cow” do not agree with the RGB scene and are unreliable, as are the tennis-racket label and some fragmented person/cellphone boundaries. This map clarifies instance separation and which objects overlap, but it supplies no dependable metric distance, facing direction, gaze, or behind/in-front ordering except where masks visibly overlap.
descriptions.pose: The pose map shows only one compact magenta hand skeleton in the first frame region, low and slightly left of centre, placing a detected hand close to the wearer’s lap and therefore roughly within 0.3–0.7 m of the camera. The finger-joint geometry gives hand orientation and articulation that are difficult to resolve in the RGB, but no yellow body skeletons and no additional hand skeletons are detected in the remaining four frames. Consequently, it provides no reliable evidence about other people’s locations, mutual distances, facing direction, gaze, reach, approach, retreat, or turning across the sequence. The lone detection is partly isolated from the visible arm/body and may be incomplete or misregistered, while hands visible near the phone and book in later frames are missed entirely.
